title: Gambler’s ruin
objectives: Solve gambler’s ruin for fair and unfair walks.

screens.prose: You have £3 and make fair £1 bets. You stop when you reach £10 or go broke. The chart shows 30 such games.
screens.question: What is the chance you reach £10 before you go broke?

options.why: You gave both ends the same chance. The broke end is 3 bets away; the target is 7 away.
You compared the two distances, 3 to 7. The chance is your share of the whole range, 3 out of 10.
That is the chance of going broke. You are nearer £0 than £10.

hints.text: Which end is closer to £3?
£0 is 3 bets away and £10 is 7 bets away.
Count the games on the chart that end at £10: about 9 of 30.

feedback.correct: In this batch 9 of the 30 games reached £10.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the games on the chart that finish at £10.

explain.text: Nine of these 30 games reached £10, close to $\tfrac{3}{10}$ of them. A fair game does not give the two ends equal chances: the nearer end is more likely. We prove the exact value, $\tfrac{3}{10}$, in two screens.

screens.prose: Same game: fair £1 bets, stop at £0 or £10. Slide your starting bankroll and watch how long the games last.
screens.question: From which starting bankroll do the games last longest?

options.why: From £1 half the games end on the very first bet.
More money helps only up to the target. From £9 one win ends the game.
Slide from £1 to £5 and compare. Games near an end stop much sooner.

hints.text: Compare the start at £1 with the start at £5.
Near either end, one short run of bets finishes the game.
The middle is furthest from both ends, so games from £5 run longest.

feedback.correct: From the middle, both ends are far away.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide the start to £1, then to £5, and compare how far right the paths reach.

explain.text: Games from the middle run longest because both ends are 5 bets away. In this batch they lasted 25 bets on average from £5, against 7 from £1. From £1 or £9 a single bet can end the game.

screens.prose: This is the **gambler's ruin** problem. Let $P_i$ be the chance of reaching £$N$ before £0, starting from £$i$. The ends are fixed: $P_0 = 0$ and $P_N = 1$. We find $P_i$ by first-step analysis.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: Condition on the first bet: $P_i = \tfrac{1}{2} P_{i+1} + \tfrac{1}{2} P_{i-1}$ for $0 < i < N$.
Multiply by 2 and rearrange: $P_{i+1} - P_i = P_i - P_{i-1}$. Every gap is the same, say $d$.

hints.text: Start with what one bet does: it moves you to $i + 1$ or $i - 1$.
The equal-gaps line rearranges the first-step equation, so it comes second.
First-step equation, equal gaps, add up the gaps from $P_0$, then use $P_N = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the first bet, and use the two ends last.

explain.text: The first-step equation says each $P_i$ is the average of its neighbours, so the $P_i$ lie on a straight line. The two ends pin the line from 0 to 1. So $P_i = i/N$, and from £3 of £10 the chance is $\tfrac{3}{10}$.

screens.prose: First-step analysis also counts the bets. Let $D_i$ be the expected number of bets from £$i$. One bet is used, then the game restarts next door: $$D_i = 1 + \tfrac{1}{2} D_{i+1} + \tfrac{1}{2} D_{i-1}, \quad D_0 = D_N = 0.$$ Its solution is $D_i = i(N - i)$.
screens.question: You start with £50 and stop at £100 or £0. How many fair £1 bets does the game last on average?

hints.text: Put $i = 50$ and $N = 100$ into $D_i = i(N - i)$.
$50 \times 50 = 2500$. Check the formula on a small case: $D_1$ with $N = 2$ is $1 \times 1 = 1$ bet.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $D_i = i(N - i)$ with $i = 50$ and $N = 100$.

byKey.distance: 50 bets would be enough only if every bet went the same way. The walk wanders back and forth.
byKey.target: 100 is the target in pounds. The walk needs far more bets than that to reach an end.
byKey.i-times-n: You used $i \times N$. The second factor is the distance to the target, $N - i = 50$.

explain.text: $D_{50} = 50 \times 50 = 2500$: the walk needs about $50^2$ bets to wander 50 away. In this batch the 20 games averaged 2,398 bets. Check the formula: $1 + \tfrac{1}{2}[(i+1)(N-i-1) + (i-1)(N-i+1)]$ simplifies to $i(N - i)$.

screens.prose: Now a casino edge: each £1 bet wins with chance $p = 0.49$. With $r = \tfrac{1-p}{p}$, first-step analysis gives $$P_i = \frac{1 - r^i}{1 - r^N}.$$ The curve shows $P_i$ for a target of £100. Slide $p$ and compare it with the dashed fair line.
screens.question: With $p = 0.49$, what is the chance of turning £50 into £100? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: First find $r = \tfrac{0.51}{0.49}$.
$r = \tfrac{51}{49} \approx 1.0408$, so $r^{50} \approx 7.39$ and $r^{100} \approx 54.6$.

feedback.correct: About 0.1192: under 12%, against 50% for a fair game.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $r = 51/49$, then $\dfrac{1 - r^{50}}{1 - r^{100}}$.

byKey.fair: That is the fair-game answer, $50/100$. The edge drags it far below.
byKey.p: 0.49 is the chance of winning one bet. Reaching £100 takes many more wins than losses on the way.
byKey.flip: 0.8808 is the answer for $p = 0.51$. You may have used $r = 49/51$; here the bets favour the casino.

explain.text: With $r = 51/49$ the formula gives about 0.1192. A 2-point edge per bet cuts the chance from 0.5 to under 0.12, because the game lasts thousands of bets. The curve sags far below the fair line in the middle.

screens.prose: You have £50 and need £100 tonight. Every bet at this table wins with chance 0.49 and pays even money. The point marks £1 bets; the dashed line marks a single bet of the whole £50.
screens.question: Which plan gives the better chance of reaching £100?

options.text: Many £1 bets, to spread the risk
options.why: You expected small bets to smooth out the edge. Over thousands of bets the edge compounds: 0.1192 against 0.49.

options.text: Both are the same, as the odds per bet are the same
options.why: The odds per bet match, but the number of bets does not. More bets give the edge more chances to work.
£10 bets are 5 steps from either end, giving about 0.450. That beats £1 bets but not one bold bet.

hints.text: How many bets does each plan need?
The single bet has chance 0.49. The £1 plan is the point on the curve.
Compare 0.49 with 0.1192.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the dashed line with the point.

byKey.small: You expected small bets to dilute the edge. They do the opposite: each bet adds a little more of it.
byKey.same: You matched the odds per bet. The plans differ in how many bets they take, and the edge acts on each one.
byKey.ten: £10 bets give 0.450, which is better than £1 bets. One bet of £50 is better still.

explain.text: When every bet loses on average, fewer bets give the edge fewer chances to work: one £50 bet gives 0.49. With the odds in your favour it flips: at $p = 0.51$, £1 bets give 0.8808 and one bet only 0.51. To reach a fixed target, bet big when the odds are against you, small when they are for you.

canvas.caption: At $p = 0.51$: £1 bets give 0.8808, one bet of £50 gives 0.51.

screens.prose: In every case you used one rule. For fair bets $P_i = \tfrac{i}{N}$; otherwise, with $r = \tfrac{1 - p}{p}$, $$P_i = \frac{1 - r^i}{1 - r^N}.$$ Now face a casino with endless money: it never runs out, so $N \to \infty$.
screens.question: With $p = 0.49$, what does your chance of eventual ruin tend to as $N \to \infty$?

options.why: That is the chance of losing one bet. Ruin needs a run of losses, but with endless time it comes.
That is the ruin chance when $p > \tfrac{1}{2}$, where $r < 1$. Here $r > 1$.
You treated the edge as too small to matter. Over endless bets even a small edge decides the game.

hints.text: With $p = 0.49$, is $r$ above or below 1?
$r = 51/49 > 1$, so $r^N$ grows without limit.
So $P_i \to 0$ as $N \to \infty$, and the chance of ruin is $1 - P_i \to 1$.

feedback.correct: Against endless money, a player with $p \le \tfrac{1}{2}$ is ruined for sure.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what $r^N$ does as $N$ grows when $r > 1$.

explain.text: With $r > 1$, $r^N \to \infty$, so $P_i \to 0$ and ruin is certain. For fair bets $P_i = i/N \to 0$ too. Only with $p > \tfrac{1}{2}$ can you survive for ever, with ruin chance $r^i$.

screens.prose: A trader has £20,000. Each trade wins or loses £1,000, and wins 49% of the time. She stops when she doubles to £40,000 or loses everything. In units of £1,000 this is gambler's ruin with $i = 20$ and $N = 40$.
screens.question: What is the chance she doubles her money before going broke? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: $r^{20} \approx 2.23$ and $r^{40} \approx 4.95$.

feedback.correct: About 0.31, not the 0.5 a fair coin would give.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count in units of £1,000, then use the unfair formula.

byKey.fair: 0.5 ignores the edge. Forty steps wide, the 49% win rate costs a lot.
byKey.p: 0.49 is one trade. Doubling takes many more wins than losses along the way.
byKey.small-bets: About 0.12 is the chance for £1 steps from 50 to 100. Here each trade is a twentieth of the bankroll, so there are fewer steps.

explain.text: With $r = 51/49$, $\dfrac{1 - r^{20}}{1 - r^{40}} \approx 0.31$. Bigger trades mean fewer steps, so the edge hurts less than with £1 bets. But a 49% strategy still loses its stake about 69% of the time.

screens.prose: A market maker's inventory moves up or down 1 lot with each trade, with equal chance. Risk limits sit at $+10$ and $-10$ lots. She starts flat and is forced to hedge when she hits a limit.
screens.question: How many trades, on average, until she first hits a limit?

hints.text: Shift the levels up by 10. Where does she start, and where are the ends?
Shifted, she starts at 10 with ends at 0 and 20.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shift the levels so the lower limit is 0, then use $D_i = i(N - i)$.

byKey.ten: 10 trades would be enough only if every trade went the same way.
byKey.twenty: 20 is the width between the limits, not the expected time to reach one.
byKey.four-hundred: You used the full width squared, $20^2$. She starts in the middle, 10 from each limit: $10 \times 10$.

explain.text: Shifting by 10 turns this into gambler's ruin from 10 with ends 0 and 20. The expected time is $10 \times 10 = 100$ trades; these 20 paths averaged 102. Doubling the limits to $\pm 20$ would make it 400 trades.

ideas: With absorbing barriers at £0 and £$N$, first-step analysis gives fair-game odds $P_i = i/N$ and expected length $i(N - i)$ bets.
With an edge, $r = (1-p)/p$ and $P_i = (1 - r^i)/(1 - r^N)$: a small edge per bet becomes a large one over many bets.
Against endless money a player with $p \le \tfrac{1}{2}$ is ruined for sure; when the odds are against you, fewer and bigger bets are better.

formula.name: Gambler’s ruin
formula.note: Fair game: $P_i = i/N$, and the expected duration is $D_i = i(N - i)$.

summary.trap: A small edge is not harmless. A 49% bet repeated thousands of times turns a 50% chance into under 12%.

quiz.prose: Fair £1 bets with target £$N$. The rule is $P_i = \tfrac{i}{N}$ and $D_i = i(N - i)$.
quiz.question: What do the rules give when you start at $i = N$?

options.why: You counted a bet at the target. The game stops as soon as you reach £$N$, so no bets are made.
The rules hold at the ends too: they are the boundary values we started from.

options.text: $P_N = \tfrac{1}{2}$: one more fair bet decides it
options.why: At £$N$ the game is over. There is no more bet to make.

feedback.correct: At the target the game is already over.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $i = N$ into both formulas.

explain.text: At $i = N$ you have reached the target, so $P_N = 1$ and no bets are needed. At $i = 0$ you are already broke: $P_0 = 0$ and $D_0 = 0$. These ends are the boundary values the derivation used.

quiz.prose: You start with £2 and make fair £1 bets until you have £8 or nothing.
quiz.question: How many bets does the game last on average?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $D_i = i(N - i)$.

byKey.prob: 0.25 is the chance of reaching £8. The question asks for the number of bets.
byKey.i-n: You used $i \times N$. The second factor is the distance to the target, $8 - 2$.
byKey.dist: 6 bets would do only if every bet won.

explain.text: $D_2 = 2 \times (8 - 2) = 12$ bets on average. The chance of reaching £8 is $\tfrac{2}{8} = 0.25$.

quiz.prose: Each bet wins with chance $p = 0.6$. You start with £2 and stop at £4 or £0.
quiz.question: What is the chance you reach £4? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $r = \tfrac{1-p}{p} = \tfrac{2}{3}$ in $\dfrac{1 - r^2}{1 - r^4}$.

byKey.fair: 0.5 is the fair-game answer. Here the bets favour you.
byKey.p: 0.6 is one bet. You need two more wins than losses before going broke.
byKey.inverted: 0.3077 is the chance of going broke. You may have used $r = p/(1-p)$.

quiz.prose: Two traders each start with £10,000 and a 49% win rate. One stakes a fixed £1,000 a trade. The other stakes 10% of whatever she has, each trade.
quiz.question: Why can the second trader never be wiped out to exactly £0?

options.text: A loss takes 10% of what is left, so 90% always remains

options.why: Both have the same 49% win rate. The difference is in the stake size.
She can trade as often as the other. Her stake shrinks as she loses, so no loss empties the account.

options.text: Proportional betting means she cannot lose money
options.why: She can lose most of her money: stakes shrink but losses still pile up. She just never reaches exactly 0.

feedback.correct: Each loss leaves 90% of the bankroll, so it shrinks but never reaches 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the bankroll after a run of losses for each trader.

explain.text: Fixed £1,000 stakes make the bankroll a walk with an absorbing barrier at 0, so gambler's ruin applies. Staking a fraction makes the bankroll multiply by 1.1 or 0.9 each trade, and a product of positive factors never hits 0. Choosing that fraction well is the Kelly question from Limits and Derivatives.
